    AI Overview
    A blockade is a, typically military, action that seals off a specific area, such as a port, coast, or region, to prevent the entry or exit of ships, aircraft, or goods. Primarily a wartime operation, it aims to cut off supplies, weaken the enemy economically, or force surrender. 
    Key Aspects of a Blockade: 
    • Military Operation: Often enforced by naval forces to control maritime, coastal, or, in modern contexts, air traffic.
    • Objective: To break an enemy's economy, cut off vital supplies, and isolate a region.
    • Legal Requirements: Under international law, a blockade must be effective (actually enforced, not just declared), impartial, and formally declared.
    • Types:
      • Naval/Commercial: Blocking shipping lanes to stop trade.
      • Land/Besieging: Surrounding a city or fort with troops to block access.
      • Economic/Protest: Using blockades (sometimes, though not always, by civilian groups) to prevent passage, such as blocking roads, ports, or fuel depots. 
    Key Differences and Details: 
    • Not a "Paper Blockade": A declaration without sufficient forces to enforce it is invalid, according to Britannica.
    • Humanitarian Concerns: Modern international law dictates that a blockade is prohibited if its sole purpose is to starve civilians, as explained on ABC News.
    • Similar Concepts: It is distinct from a "siege," which focuses on surrounding a specific fortification, though they often coincide, as noted on Wikipedia.

    Definitions from Oxford Languages · Learn more
    block·ade
    /ˌbläˈkād/
    Learn to pronounce
    noun
    noun: blockade; plural noun: blockades
    1. an act or means of sealing off a place to prevent goods or people from entering or leaving.
      "there was a blockade of humanitarian aid"
      h
      Similar:
      siege
      beleaguerment
      encirclement
      investment
      besiegement
      barricade
      barrier
      roadblock
      obstacle
      obstruction
      impediment
      bulwark
      block
      hindrance
      check
      deterrent
      hurdle
      • an obstruction of a physiological or mental function, especially of a biochemical receptor.
    verb
    verb: blockade; 3rd person present: blockades; past tense: blockaded; past participle: blockaded; gerund or present participle: blockading
    1. seal off (a place) to prevent goods or people from entering or leaving.
      "the authorities blockaded roads in and out of the capital"
      h
      Similar:
      barricade
      close up
      block off
      shut off
      seal
      bar
      besiege
      lay siege to
      beleaguer
      beset
      surround
      invest
    Phrases
    run a blockade — (of a ship) manage to enter or leave a blockaded port.
    "vessels suspected of running the UN blockade"
    Origin
    late 17th century: from block + -ade1, probably influenced by ambuscade .
    Use over time for: blockade

    What is a blockade in simple terms?
    A blockade is an obstacle that stands between you and something you're trying to reach. After a robbery, police might set up a blockade around the neighborhood to catch the thief. Anything that impedes or halts progress is a blockade.

    What is a blockade in US history?
    A wartime blockade used to mean a naval patrol of an enemy seaport to stop all sea traffic. Today it means any barrier to the passage of people, supplies, or communications in or out of a country.

    Are blockades legal in war?
    According to modern international law, blockades are an act of war. In that sense, a blockade can be legal only if applied in the context self-defense – but never as part of a war of aggression.
